caption:
Four current and former Kenwood High School students sued Omnilert, Baltimore County schools and police on November 17.
In October 2025, Omnilert's AI flagged a bag of Doritos as a gun with a 90 percent probability. Staff canceled the alert, but armed officers came anyway and handcuffed the students.
They want every AI alert checked by a person before police are sent.

Should schools use AI to watch for guns?

threads_text: Four students in Baltimore County are suing after an AI camera system flagged a bag of Doritos as a gun and armed police handcuffed them, even though staff had already canceled the alert. Should schools trust AI to call the police?

paragraphs.text: Four current and former students of Kenwood High School in Baltimore County, Maryland, sued the AI company Omnilert, Baltimore County Public Schools, school officials, the Baltimore County Police Department and individual officers on November 17, 2026. The suit, filed in Baltimore County Circuit Court, centers on an October 2025 incident in which Omnilert's weapon detection system flagged a bag of chips as a possible gun and armed officers detained the students.

The students, who are Black, are represented by the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, working with the law firms Willkie Farr & Gallagher and Engel Law Group, according to USA Today. TheGrio reported that the complaint runs 31 pages and accuses the defendants of violating the students' federal and state constitutional rights, along with negligence and gross negligence.

According to USA Today, the students were waiting outside the school for a ride home after football practice on October 20, 2025. Omnilert's AI system, which watches school camera feeds for firearms, sent an alert that reported a 90 percent probability that a gun was present. The object in one student's hand was a bag of Cool Ranch Doritos.

School staff and a police representative reviewed the image, judged that there was no gun and canceled the alert, the suit and a state review say. Armed officers were dispatched anyway. Attorneys for the students said officers surrounded them, many with guns drawn, ordered them to their knees, handcuffed them and searched them. No weapon was found. Police body camera footage obtained by WBFF Fox45 later showed officers finding a chip bag in a nearby trash can.

A November 2025 report by the Maryland Office of the Inspector General for Education found that a school employee missed the cancellation and passed a screenshot of the alert to a law enforcement officer, which set off the police response. The report attributed the incident to human error and training gaps, found no evidence that the system discriminated by race, and said the alert was triggered by the student's position, hand movements and the reflective qualities of the object rather than by recognizing a chip bag.

The suit does not name a dollar amount in damages, according to USA Today and the Baltimore Chronicle. It asks for procedures that require schools and police to verify AI threat alerts before acting, policies that keep false alerts from triggering armed police responses, and more training, oversight and transparency. The Baltimore Chronicle reported that it also asks for an evaluation of whether AI weapon detection belongs in schools at all.

Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers' Committee, said the students were "failed not only by a technology that is prone to false alerts." Freida Winfield, a parent who was picking up her son that day, said no child in Baltimore County should face that kind of danger while waiting outside school. The Baltimore County Police Department told USA Today it could not comment on pending litigation, and the school system and Omnilert had not publicly responded.

Baltimore County Public Schools signed a four year, $2.6 million contract with Omnilert in 2023, and it runs until 2027. After the incident, Omnilert told WBFF that the system functioned as intended, and Superintendent Myriam Rogers said alerts must be verified by people before police respond. Weeks later, another Omnilert alert sent police to Parkville High School, where no weapon was found. Separately, a survivor of a 2025 shooting at Antioch High School in Tennessee sued Omnilert in May 2026, alleging that the same kind of system failed to detect the shooter's gun.

The case puts the hardest question about AI security tools in front of a court: who is responsible when a machine's guess becomes an armed police response. The state review blamed people and process rather than the software, while the students argue that the whole chain, from vendor to school to police, failed together. How the court divides that responsibility could shape how schools across the country write rules for acting on AI alerts.

The Baltimore County school board has to decide before the contract ends in 2027 whether to renew, change or drop Omnilert, and the first court response from the defendants will show how they plan to answer the claims.
